props.title: What Time Is It There?
props.initialSlug: A lonely watchmaker obsesses over Paris time

sections.content: Tsai Ming-liang's meditative What Time Is It There? masterfully explores time, loss and connection across continents. After his father's death, a Taipei street vendor becomes obsessed with setting every clock he encounters to Paris time, while simultaneously selling his dual-time watch to a young woman departing for France. The film builds on Tsai's signature style established in Rebels of the Neon God (1992) and The River (1997) - long, static takes, minimal dialogue, and an almost hypnotic attention to mundane activities that reveal deeper emotional currents.

sections.content: The film's parallel structure between Taipei and Paris creates a fascinating study in global disconnection. While Chungking Express (1994) used similar themes of international longing more kinetically, Tsai's approach is deliberately slower, more haunting. The influence of French New Wave cinema, particularly Francois Truffaut's work, emerges in both visual references and thematic concerns about time and memory.

The performances by Lee Kang-sheng (Tsai's longtime collaborator) and Chen Shiang-chyi embody a peculiarly modern form of alienation. Their characters' inability to connect despite technology mirrors later works like Lost in Translation (2003) and Cafe Lumiere (2003), though Tsai's approach is far more minimalist and challenging. SUBHEAD: Time, Memory and Urban Spaces

movies.title: I Don't Want to Sleep Alone
movies.slug: A mysterious stranger is cared for by locals in Kuala Lumpur, examining connection and alienation

sections.content: Tsai's use of urban spaces - empty apartments, crowded streets, anonymous hotels - creates a distinct vocabulary of modern loneliness. Like fellow Asian auteurs Wong Kar-wai in In the Mood for Love (2000) and Edward Yang in Yi Yi (2000), he transforms city spaces into emotional landscapes. The repeated motif of clocks and time zones becomes both literal and metaphysical, suggesting the impossibility of truly synchronized human connection.
